intro: Read the deck for the content and these notes for the thinking. Each note explains a slide, gives you a way to remember it or warns you where fieldworkers slip. Work the examples in pencil, answer the recall questions with the page covered, and write your own marginal notes beside mine.

sections.title: What Is Visual Ethnography?
sections.big_idea: Visual ethnography uses images as **evidence you analyse**. A picture you could never let change your conclusion is decoration.
in_plain_words: Ethnography studies a culture from the inside. Visual ethnography does this through images, whether photographs, video, drawings or objects, and treats them as data, as a way of generating knowledge and as a way of sharing findings. The camera is a research instrument and a social act, so it needs the care you give an interview guide.

Images capture texture, arrangement and the taken-for-granted. Words capture motive, sequence and cause. The method works best when the two travel together. In South Asia, where calendar art, wedding photographs, murals and **WhatsApp forwards** are everywhere, participants are already skilled readers of images.

diagram.caption: three uses and three kinds of visual world

key_terms.meaning: Study of culture in which images produce, analyse and communicate knowledge.
The image is evidence to be read, including what it omits.
Making the image is how knowledge is generated, as in photovoice.
Images communicate findings to an audience.
An existing image such as an album, poster or signage.
What people never mention, which images record without effort.

worked_example.title: Is this visual ethnography?
worked_example.setup: Apply the slide 4 test to three cases: could the image change your conclusion?
steps: Case A: stock photos dropped into a report to fill space. No relationship, no analysis, so no.
Case B: you photograph a market, ask vendors to photograph their day, then build a photo-essay. Data, method and output are all present, so yes.
Case C: images are gathered and captioned but never read. They are decoration with a methods section attached, so no.
Apply the test: would any photograph you might have taken have altered the finding?
worked_example.answer: Only Case B qualifies; A and C are illustration.

mistakes: Treating images as illustration for a written report. The deck's definition requires systematic analysis.
Choosing images for appeal. Aesthetic selection is not analytic selection.
Assuming an image can state a cause or a sequence. Words are needed for that, which is why the method pairs them.
Treating a donor photo shoot as fieldwork. There the subject is a prop for an audience elsewhere.

recall.q: What are the three uses of images in the deck?
recall.a: As data, as method and as output.

recall.q: What can images capture that words struggle with?
recall.a: Texture, spatial arrangement, gesture and posture, and the taken-for-granted.

recall.q: What is the test that an image counts as evidence?
recall.a: Whether it could change your conclusion.

recall.q: Name three categories of the visual world.
recall.a: Made, found and lived.

recall.q: Why has consent to cover circulation as well as capture?
recall.a: Subjects own cameras and images circulate instantly, so where it ends up matters.

sections.title: A Short History
sections.big_idea: The camera arrived with empire and anthropology, so its habits of **classifying, posing and naming types** still shape donor photographs today.
in_plain_words: Photography began in 1839 and grew up beside modern anthropology. Early work posed people as specimens, used measuring grids and rarely named them. In colonial South Asia, projects such as The People of India (1868–75) catalogued castes and tribes as types, and the salvage frame treated living communities as vanishing relics.

Change came in steps. Bateson and Mead used 759 photographs as analysable data in 1942, and Collier named photo-elicitation and made the camera a research tool. Sontag and Berger then argued that **seeing is never neutral**. The collaborative turn moved the camera to the community, but handing over the lens does not by itself hand over editing, publishing or copyright.

events.what: The People of India catalogues types

key_terms.meaning: Using the camera to classify, measure and control people.
Recording 'vanishing' cultures, freezing living peoples as relics.
Frontal, unnamed portraits that treat a person as a type.
Using photographs to prompt interviews, named by Collier.
Moving from objectifying to partnering with the people photographed.
The harm of an archive that told people who they were in a form the state could use.

worked_example.title: Spot the old grammar in a modern photograph
worked_example.setup: An NGO report shows a woman photographed from above, unnamed, with a caption written by the organisation.
steps: Name the row: she is unnamed, so the person becomes a type.
Name the next: posed to signify need, so the picture is arranged for an audience.
Name the third: the caption carries the organisation's meaning, so she has no say.
Choose the fix from slide 20: name her with consent, let her say what the caption says and give her the photograph.
worked_example.answer: Three rows of the colonial grammar repeat; all three can be fixed at no cost.

mistakes: Believing the camera simply captures truth. The deck says every image is made by someone, for someone.
Assuming salvage logic ended in 1930. A grant proposal to document a 'disappearing craft' uses the same frame.
Counting a participatory project as collaborative because people hold the camera. Check who edits, who publishes and who holds copyright.
Citing Sontag and Berger as arguments against photography. Both argued against treating it as transparent.

recall.q: What was The People of India (1868–75)?
recall.a: A colonial project that photographed communities as types, captioned by category.

recall.q: How many photographs did Balinese Character (1942) analyse?
Which technique did John Collier Jr. name?
recall.a: Photo-elicitation.

recall.q: What does Berger's point direct you to ask?
recall.a: Whose way of seeing a given image encodes.

recall.q: Give two rows where the old gaze differs from the collaborative turn.
recall.a: For example, the subject moves from specimen to partner, and power moves from outward and extractive to shared and negotiated.

sections.title: The Methods Map
sections.big_idea: Every method is an answer to three questions: **who makes the image, in what medium and for what**. The first carries the most weight.
in_plain_words: Visual methods fall into three families by who produces the image: the researcher, the participant, or an existing source such as an album or archive. Each has a strength and a weakness. Researcher images give coverage and comparison, participant images give priorities you would not guess, and archives give change over time.

Photo-elicitation and video are not families. They cut across all three. Most projects mix methods, which improves the work, but you must label the set so a reader knows **who held the camera**. Choose the method by the question you ask, and remember that photovoice and participatory video are the expensive rows.

diagram.caption: photo-elicitation uses any of these to prompt talk

key_terms.meaning: The same frame photographed at intervals to show change.
Images made by the people you study, showing their priorities.
An existing image that you analyse instead of making.
Elicitation using photographs of the participant themselves.
Using old photographs or records to prompt memory.
Combining families, such as participant photos plus your survey.

worked_example.title: Count the design choices
worked_example.setup: Slide 22 lists the options for each question: who makes it (3), which medium (4) and what it is for (3).
steps: Options for who: researcher, participant, already exists, which is 3.
Options for medium: photo, video, drawing, object, which is 4.
Options for purpose: data, method, output, which is 3.
Possible combinations: 3 × 4 × 3 = 36.
Write your choice for all three before fieldwork.
worked_example.answer: 36 combinations, which is why the three answers must be written down in advance.

mistakes: Choosing the medium first and the purpose later. You end with a large image archive and no analytic use for it.
Mixing families without labelling them. A reader will assume you held the camera.
Judging participant photographs on technical craft. Their value lies in what they reveal.
Treating photovoice or participatory video as a cheap route to photographs. They cost training, equipment and weeks of facilitation.

recall.q: What are the three questions that organise every method?
recall.a: Who makes the image, what medium, and what for.

recall.q: Which technique is repeat photography?
recall.a: Photographing the same frame at intervals to show change over time.

recall.q: What does handing over the camera reveal about what is not photographed?
recall.a: The refusals often map risk, shame and privacy.

recall.q: Why is photo-elicitation not a fourth family?
recall.a: It is a technique that takes images from any family.

recall.q: Which method does the slide call highest return for limited time?
recall.a: Photo-elicitation.

sections.title: Photo-Elicitation
sections.big_idea: In photo-elicitation **the talk is the data** and the photograph is the instrument that produces it.
in_plain_words: Photo-elicitation puts photographs on the table during an interview. Collier observed that images sharpen memory and lengthen interviews. A shared object gives both people somewhere to look, so silence is comfortable, the participant leads and disagreement is easier. The images can be yours, for comparison, or theirs, for priorities and meaning.

A good interview runs in five stages: select, open, probe, connect, close. You ask and the participant interprets. Use about a dozen images, prefer prints and record which image prompted which answer. Watch for **leading images, embarrassing photographs and assumed meanings**, and ask what is happening before you ask what it means.

diagram.caption: the five stages of an elicitation interview

key_terms.meaning: An interview in which photographs prompt and shape the talk.
Elicitation using images the participant made or owns.
A photograph that plants your interpretation in the participant's answer.
'What is happening here?' asked before any question about meaning.
Memory of a scene, which photographs recruit more than summary questions do.
Shaped by both people; the images you bring influence the story you hear.

worked_example.title: Plan one interview
worked_example.setup: You will interview a woman about water collection using photographs. Illustrative: assume about 5 minutes of talk per image.
steps: Select a manageable set of 12 images instead of a hundred, and bring spares so she can choose.
Time needed: 12 × 5 = 60 minutes.
Open with 'Tell me about this one' and let her lead.
Ask the closing question: 'What would you have photographed that is not here?'
Note which image prompted each answer so the transcript links back to the picture.
worked_example.answer: About 60 minutes for 12 images, with a record linking each answer to its image.

mistakes: Analysing the images and discarding the transcript. The talk is the data and the technique has been used backwards.
Showing a hundred images. Fatigue destroys the depth you came for.
Telling the participant what a photograph means. The golden rule is that you ask and they interpret.
Quoting a percentage for the effect. The deck says only that interviews tend to run longer and richer, which is defensible, while a figure is not.

recall.q: Who introduced photo-elicitation?
recall.a: John Collier Jr., in the 1950s and 1960s.

recall.q: What are the five stages of the interview?
recall.a: Select, open, probe, connect and close.

recall.q: Why are prints better than screens?
recall.a: A print can be held, sorted, set aside and returned to, so the participant takes part in the interview and does more than watch.

recall.q: What risk does the third failure row describe?
recall.a: Assuming an image means the same to them as to you.

recall.q: Which images should be run first if you use both?
recall.a: The participant's, so their framing is set before your categories arrive.

sections.title: Photovoice
sections.big_idea: Photovoice is built to reach decision-makers. **Photography without an audience that can act** has produced an exhibition.
in_plain_words: Photovoice is a participatory action research method formalised by Wang and Burris in 1997 from work with rural women in Yunnan. Participants photograph their own lives, discuss the images collectively and take them to people who can act. It draws on Freire, feminist theory and documentary photography, and it has three goals: record, dialogue and reach.

The SHOWeD questions guide the discussion from describing a photograph to naming causes and planning action. The W, why the situation exists, is the hinge. Run the six-stage process with ethics training first and budget the exhibition early. The method gives depth, and it cannot give **representativeness**: twelve photographers are twelve people's priorities.

diagram.caption: SHOWeD, read from the bottom up

key_terms.meaning: Participants use cameras to document their lives and take the images to decision-makers.
Six questions: See, Happening, Our lives, Why, educate, Do.
Freire's idea of reflection leading to action.
Research used as a route to change.
Involving people without letting them shape outcomes.
First session: consent from those photographed, risk and safety.

worked_example.title: Audit a project against the three goals
worked_example.setup: A project trains twelve women, runs a camera week and holds a group discussion with SHOWeD. It never invites an official.
steps: Goal 1, record strengths and concerns: delivered by the photography.
Goal 2, promote critical dialogue: delivered by the facilitated discussion.
Goal 3, reach policymakers: not delivered, as no one who can act was in the room.
Goals delivered: 2 ÷ 3 = 0.67.
The slide says to plan the audience before shooting, so fix it by inviting decision-makers to an exhibition.
worked_example.answer: Two of three goals are met. Without the third it should not be called photovoice to a funder.

mistakes: Running the photography and discussion and skipping the route to decision-makers.
Letting the facilitator name the content at the See stage, which closes the question for the group.
Accepting an answer to Why that stops at individual blame. The Do that follows will be a list of self-improvement tasks.
Handing out cameras before ethics training. Consent obligations transfer to participants with the camera.

recall.q: Who formalised photovoice, and when?
recall.a: Caroline Wang and Mary Ann Burris, in 1997.

recall.q: What are the three goals?
recall.a: Record, promote critical dialogue and reach policymakers.

recall.q: What does SHOWeD stand for?
recall.a: See, Happening, Our lives, Why, educate, Do.

recall.q: Which stage is the most under-resourced?
recall.a: Exhibiting to decision-makers.

recall.q: What can photovoice not provide?
recall.a: Representativeness, since participants are a selected group.

sections.title: Video & Film Methods
sections.big_idea: Video captures time, movement and sound, but costs far more to make, analyse and **anonymise**. Use it when sequence is the point.
in_plain_words: Video suits ritual, work processes, interaction and embodied skill. Observational video keeps the researcher behind the lens; participatory video trains the group to plan, shoot and screen their own films. A minute of usable film can cost a day of work, because logging, transcribing and editing come after the fieldwork, when the budget is usually spent.

Editing is interpretation: what you keep, cut and sequence builds the argument, and sequence manufactures causation. Faces, voices and places are hard to anonymise, and footage can circulate indefinitely, so consent must name every venue. The community screening is part of the method and should happen **before the film is finalised**.

key_terms.meaning: Filming events as they unfold with minimal intrusion.
A facilitator trains a group to make their own films.
Indexing footage with timecodes so it can be searched and coded.
An early edit shown to participants for objection and correction.
Showing the film to the community as data, validation and action.
Ongoing agreement covering screening, online use, archiving and withdrawal.

worked_example.title: Cost a short film
worked_example.setup: Slide 51 says a minute of usable film can cost a day of work. Use that as the rule for a planned 10-minute film.
steps: Usable minutes planned: 10.
Days of work at the slide's rule: 10 × 1 = 10 days.
Add community members' time in front of and behind the camera as paid, respected work.
If the logging cannot be funded, the slide's advice is to drop the video.
worked_example.answer: About 10 days of work, before counting community members' hours.

mistakes: Budgeting the shooting days and not the logging. The footage then sits unanalysed.
Calling observational film 'fly on the wall'. A camera in the room is an event in that room.
Handing over the camera and keeping the edit. That is participation in the shooting only.
Treating consent as a signature. Agreement to a community screening does not cover a website, and the second cannot be undone.

recall.q: When should you choose video over stills?
recall.a: When sequence and timing, speech and gesture, or a skill or process carry the meaning.

recall.q: What are the four steps of participatory video in practice?
recall.a: Games and camera training, group storyboarding, filming and review, and a community screening.

recall.q: What builds the argument in an edit?
recall.a: What is cut, since the argument is made by omission as well as selection.

recall.q: Why is video hard to anonymise?
recall.a: Voice, gait, a courtyard or a name spoken off camera can identify a person even if the face is blurred.

recall.q: What should the community screening be recorded for?
recall.a: Reactions and corrections, which are often the richest material.

sections.title: Working With Images in the Field
sections.big_idea: Settle purpose, consent and storage **before you press the shutter**, then record context, because an image without it is a riddle.
in_plain_words: Before shooting, decide what the images are for, secure community and individual permission, plan consent in the local language, set limits on what you will photograph and fix storage and deletion. Gatekeeper permission is not individual consent. Consent to photograph and consent to publish are collected separately.

In the field, framing carries meaning, and the same queue at a water point can mean scarcity, early rising or system failure. Log metadata and fieldnotes for every image, including what you could not photograph. The camera changes the scene, so spend time until it is ordinary. Stop collecting at **saturation for a question**, with depth ahead of volume.

key_terms.meaning: Free, understood agreement covering capture, use, venue and withdrawal.
Access granted by a leader, which cannot stand in for individual consent.
Date, place, people, consent status and the prompt that made the image.
People tidy, pose, withdraw or perform when a lens is present.
The point where new images stop revealing new themes for a question.
India's law covering identifiable personal data held digitally, photographs included.

worked_example.title: Write the log row
worked_example.setup: You photograph a queue at a water point at 5 a.m. and someone in the frame agreed to be photographed but not to publication.
steps: File name and date and time: record 5 a.m., since the hour is part of the meaning.
Location and the event: the water point and the prompt for the shot.
Who is shown: name or code, so a withdrawal can be honoured.
Consent status and scope: photographed yes, publication no, recorded against this image.
Caption notes and fieldnote: why you took it and what you could not photograph.
worked_example.answer: A complete row keeps the 5 a.m. context and blocks accidental publication.

mistakes: Treating the sarpanch's permission as consent for the woman in the frame.
Recording consent against the visit and not against each image. Later nobody knows which photographs a person agreed to.
Publishing a photograph with embedded GPS, which can identify a household.
Collecting a target number of images. Saturation is specific to a question and cannot be set in advance.

recall.q: Why must photograph consent and publication consent be asked separately?
recall.a: The second has consequences and needs its own conversation about use, venue and duration.

recall.q: Name three fields in the image log.
recall.a: Any of: date, location, who is shown, consent status, the prompt or event, caption notes.

recall.q: What does a low angle usually read as?
recall.a: Dignity and stature.

recall.q: What is the sign that you have reached saturation?
recall.a: New images stop revealing new themes and you can predict what the next will show.

recall.q: Which obligation is cheapest and most often promised but not done?
recall.a: Returning prints to the people photographed.

notes.2: Skim the agenda before you start. Slide 11 groups these sections into the methods (history through field practice) and the judgement (analysis, ethics, dignity and presenting). Choose the section you most need and read it first, then return to the rest in order.
notes.4: Hold onto the test at the bottom: could an image change your conclusion? If no photograph would have altered the finding, the pictures are decoration. Use the table as a quick audit of your own project by ticking which column each of your images belongs in.
notes.5: Images and words do different jobs, so plan for both. Photographs hold texture, arrangement and the taken-for-granted. Words hold motive, sequence and cause. The strongest argument for the method is the last row: the ordinary arrangement of a room, which no interview would produce.
notes.6: Ask which of the three roles an image plays before you shoot it: data, method or output. The middle one is the one people forget. In photovoice the talk about why a picture was taken is the data, and it exists only because the camera was there.
notes.7: Use this as a rejection list. If your images are stock fillers, chosen for beauty, taken without consent or staged for a donor, they belong in the second column. The last row is the one practitioners actually do. The question that sorts them is whether the person had a say.
notes.8: Widen your idea of an image. Made, found and lived images all count, and the found category is cheap: what a household hangs on its wall tells you about aspiration or religion with no photography at all. Remember the caution that publicly posted does not mean available for your purposes.
notes.9: South Asia gives you ready research sites. Learn the examples as pairs of image and meaning, such as calendar art with household religion, or NREGA muster boards with transparency. The key point is that participants are fluent readers of images, probably sharper ones than you assume.
notes.10: The chart is illustrative, so quote the trend without the numbers. Your participants carry cameras too, and a photo from a village can be on a screen in Delhi within the hour. So consent must cover circulation, and being the only camera in the room needs a reason.
notes.11: Slide 11 is your reading plan. Each section answers one question, listed in the table. If you have limited time, the slide recommends three sections: the methods map, analysis and ethics. Their absence shows in the output more than any other.
notes.13: Photography and anthropology grew up together in one century, and the early habits show. The table lists four practices with the assumption behind each. Look for them in a modern frontal, unnamed portrait of a beneficiary, which repeats the specimen convention without intending to.
notes.14: The People of India (1868–75) is the example to remember: communities photographed as types, captioned by category, compiled after 1857 and circulated to administrators. The slide's point is that photographic classification helped make colonial categories real. Know this before you photograph anyone as a representative of a group.
notes.15: Salvage ethnography sounds caring and removes the present from people. Use the slide's test on your own proposals: does your project record what people say they want to keep, change or abandon? If it does not, you are salvaging. Phrases like 'last generation of speakers' are the warning sign.
notes.16: Bateson and Mead's 759 photographs mark the point where images became analysable data with explicit selection criteria, so credit that. Then read the second paragraph: the Balinese were studied as subjects and never worked as collaborators, and the categories belonged to the researchers.
notes.17: Collier is where the method takes shape: the camera as a disciplined research tool, and photo-elicitation as a named technique. Read the table with the claim on the left and the permission it gave on the right. The slide advises reading Collier for craft and the critics for what the craft cannot see.
notes.18: Memorise the shift as five rows: who holds the camera, what the subject is, what the image is, which way power flows, and the goal. Then apply the warning below the table. Handing over the camera changes who frames, and it leaves editing, publishing and copyright untouched.
notes.19: Use the two critics as questions. Sontag asks what the act of photographing takes from its subject, and Berger asks whose way of seeing the image encodes. The slide says Berger's question is the more useful in practice because it has an answer you can look for.
notes.20: This slide bridges history and your own practice. Go down the table and check an NGO photograph against each row: unnamed, posed, captioned by the organisation, used elsewhere and never returned. Every row has a free fix, so decide which ones you will adopt before you start.
notes.22: Answer three questions in writing before fieldwork: who makes the image, in what medium and for what purpose. The first carries the most weight because it decides whose priorities appear. Projects that choose the medium first end up with a large archive and nothing to do with it.
notes.23: Learn the map as three columns by who produces the image, with photo-elicitation cutting across all of them. The table gives each family's strength and weakness. Mixing is normal, so label every set with who held the camera. Otherwise readers will assume it was you.
notes.24: Researcher-produced images give control and consistency, and the frame reflects your assumptions. The technique to take from this slide is repeat photography: the same frame at intervals shows change that no single image or memory can establish. Pair it with participant work to find what you missed.
notes.25: Handing over the camera reveals priorities you would not guess. The finding people overlook is in the third row: what participants choose to leave unphotographed. Ask about those refusals, because they map risk, shame and privacy. Expect imperfect images, and judge them on what they reveal.
notes.26: Found images are cheap and rich. Learn the table of what to read in each type, from family albums to government photographs. The NGO archive is the uncomfortable one, since twenty years of photographs show how the organisation has seen people. Found images also carry the heaviest consent problems.
notes.27: Photo-elicitation is a technique that works with images from any family, and video cuts across them too. Keep the ethical point: consent and harm travel with the image. Decide in advance what you will do if showing a photograph produces distress instead of talk.
notes.28: Use this as your decision table and match the question you have to the method. Photo-elicitation is the highest-return choice when time is short, because it needs only images you already have. Choose photovoice and participatory video when participation is the aim, since they cost training, equipment and weeks.
notes.30: In this method the talk is the data and the photograph is the instrument. Studies that analyse the images and discard the transcript have used the technique backwards. A poor photograph works if the participant recognises it and it is relevant. The table lists the roles the image plays.
notes.31: A photograph recruits specific memory, which a bare question cannot. The third row is underrated: a shared object gives both people somewhere to look, so pauses become comfortable, and pauses are where the material arrives. Plan to let silence run when you use this method.
notes.32: The chart is illustrative, so say only that photo-prompted interviews tend to run longer and richer. The slide warns against quoting a percentage. The second table matters just as much: an image does not repair mistrust, and it does not make people answer questions they have reason to avoid.
notes.33: Choose whose photographs go on the table. Yours give comparison and risk planting a frame. Theirs give priorities and cannot be aggregated. The slide suggests running their images first and yours second, so their framing is established before your categories arrive.
notes.34: Memorise the five stages: select, open, probe, connect, close. The golden rule is that the participant interprets the image and you ask. The best question is the last one: what would you have photographed that is not here? Record which image prompted each answer.
notes.35: This is the method at work. One photograph of a distant handpump opened talk of time, safety, girls' schooling and caste access to the well. A direct survey question would have flattened all of that. Keep it as the example you give when someone asks why bother with images.
notes.36: These are craft rules with reasons. A dozen images, because fatigue destroys depth. Prints, because a participant can hold and sort them. And a note of which image prompted what. Bring more images than you use, and watch what the participant picks up first and what they never touch.
notes.37: Four failure modes, each with a prevention. The cross-cultural one is the third row: you read poverty where they read an ordinary house. Ask 'what is happening here?' before you ask what it means, and have a local person review your set before you use it.
notes.39: Photovoice has three elements the slide stresses: participants choose the subjects, the group discusses the images and the work reaches decision-makers. The common failure is skipping the third. A project with no route to officials has produced an exhibition, which should not be described to a funder as photovoice.
notes.40: The lineage explains the design: Freire's critical consciousness, feminist theory, documentary photography and participatory action research. It was built to reach policymakers, so a project that stops at photography has implemented one third of the method. Remember 1997, Yunnan, and Wang and Burris.
notes.41: Three goals: record, dialogue and reach. The table shows the third is skipped very often, and it is the one that separates photovoice from a photography workshop. Plan the audience before the shooting, because deciding later usually means showing the work to whoever is available.
notes.42: SHOWeD is six questions asked of each chosen photograph: See, Happening, Our lives, Why, educate, Do. Say the letters aloud until they stick. The table lists how each stage goes wrong, and the facilitator's job is to ask, wait and let the second and third answers come.
notes.43: The framework moves a group from description to causes to action. The W is the critical step and the one facilitators rush. A group that answers it with individual failings will produce a list of self-improvement tasks. Keep the S too, because description lets everyone enter.
notes.44: Six stages run from recruiting to acting. Training in ethics matters because the consent duties pass to participants along with the camera. The table shows the exhibition is the most under-resourced stage, so the slide's advice is to budget it first.
notes.45: Safety is the first session. Participants need consent from those they photograph, and photographing power can endanger them: an illegal dump, a contractor, the police. Work through what is safe to photograph as a group, because the participants know that and you do not.
notes.46: Read strengths and limits as pairs, each strength with its matching limit, such as marginalised voices from a selected group. Photovoice gives depth and cannot give representativeness, so say so in any report. Twelve participants' photographs are twelve people's priorities.
notes.48: Choose video when motion and sequence are the point, and stills when anonymity or a place matters. Video is roughly an order of magnitude more work per hour of material. It is also the hardest to anonymise, since a voice, a gait or a courtyard can identify a participant.
notes.49: Observational and participatory video are ends of a spectrum. 'Fly on the wall' is an aspiration, because a camera in a room is an event in that room. The fourth row, skills left behind, is what makes participatory video expensive and worth it.
notes.50: Participatory video follows four steps: games and camera training, group storyboarding, filming and review, and a community screening. The facilitator trains and the group makes the film. Remember the outcome the slide names: confidence and a tool the community keeps.
notes.51: A minute of usable film can cost a day of work, so cost the whole chain: planning, capture, logging, transcription, editing and community members' time. The slide's hard rule is plain. If you cannot fund the logging, do not shoot the video.
notes.52: Editing is where meaning is made. What you keep builds the evidence, what you cut builds the argument and the sequence builds causation, since two shots in order read as cause and effect. In participatory video whoever edits holds the meaning, so show participants the rough cut.
notes.53: Video raises the stakes on anonymity, circulation, consent scope and withdrawal. Write the venues into the consent, because agreeing to a community screening does not cover a website, and the second cannot be undone. Agree an expiry and a deletion date in writing.
notes.54: Follow the five steps in order: log, transcribe, note gesture and gaze, code, return to the footage. Log before you code, since memory over-weights the striking moments. The slide adds a test. If you use only the transcript, an audio recorder would have done.
notes.55: The screening is part of the method. Reactions, arguments and corrections there are data, validation and action at once, so record it. Show the film to the community before finalising it, because a first screening at a donor event closes the loop with the wrong audience.
notes.57: Settle five things before you press the shutter: purpose, permissions, consent in the local language, what you will not photograph, and storage. The sharpest warning is that gatekeeper permission is not individual consent. A sarpanch cannot consent for the woman in the frame.
notes.58: Visual consent covers what is captured, where it appears, for how long, whether people are named and how to withdraw. Ask separately for consent to be photographed and consent to publish. The slide notes the DPDP Act covers photographs of identifiable people, so retention and deletion become legal questions.
notes.59: Framing is an interpretive choice. Use the table as a decoder: low angle reads as stature, high angle as diminishment, tight crop as intimacy or exposure, wide as a person in a life. An isolated subject with no background reads as a type, the donor-photograph convention.
notes.60: The water-queue example shows one image supporting four meanings, and the caption decides which. So record who, what, where, when and what happened before and after. The danger the slide names is publishing a photograph of an unusual day as if it were typical.
notes.61: Build the log as you go: file name, date, place, people, consent reference and caption notes. Record consent against each image and not only the visit. Phone photographs carry GPS, which helps your record and can identify a household if you publish the file with it.
notes.62: Write fieldnotes beside the images: why you took the shot, what you could not photograph, how people reacted to the camera and what happened around it. The refusals row is the most valuable. Write the notes the same day, since later reconstruction produces the caption you want.
notes.63: The camera co-creates the scene. People tidy, pose, withdraw or perform. In development settings some perform need or its opposite because they think a photograph affects eligibility, which the slide treats as rational. The effect fades with repeat visits, so a camera on the fourth visit records something closer to routine.
notes.64: Care is a list of promises you can keep: secure backups, consent stored with the images, prints returned, deletion done. The last row, planning for the archive to outlive the project, is the one nobody plans. Budget the prints as a line item.
notes.65: Stop when new images stop revealing new themes. Saturation is specific to one question: you can be saturated on how a water point is used and far from it on who never goes there. The slide's rule is depth over volume, so thirty images made with care beat a thousand without consent.
